question: In which year was the Lodi dynasty, the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, founded?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1451.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Lodi dynasty was founded in 1451 by Bahlul Lodi, who deposed the last Sayyid ruler, Alam Shah. (लोदी वंश — 1451)

 

• It was the fifth and last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, and the first Afghan (Pashtun) dynasty to rule Delhi — the four before it having been of Turkish or Sayyid descent.

 

• Its three rulers were Bahlul Lodi (1451-89), Sikandar Lodi (1489-1517) and Ibrahim Lodi (1517-26).

 

• The dynasty and the Sultanate ended together at the First Battle of Panipat, 21 April 1526, where Babur defeated and killed Ibrahim Lodi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate:

 

• Slave / Mamluk – 1206-1290 (Qutb-ud-din Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia, Balban)

 

• Khalji – 1290-1320 (Jalal-ud-din, Alauddin Khalji)

 

• Tughlaq – 1320-1414 (Ghiyas-ud-din, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firoz Shah)

 

• Sayyid – 1414-1451 (Khizr Khan)

 

• Lodi – 1451-1526

 

• Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra in 1504 and moved his capital there. Ibrahim Lodi is the only Sultan of Delhi to have died on the battlefield.

 

NOTE

 

• 1414 (Option 2): The year the Sayyid dynasty was founded by Khizr Khan, a former governor under Timur — the dynasty that the Lodis displaced.

 

• 1489 (Option 3): The year Sikandar Lodi, the second and ablest ruler of the line, came to the throne.

 

• 1517 (Option 4): The year Ibrahim Lodi, the last of the line, succeeded Sikandar.

question: In the administration of the Delhi Sultanate, land assigned to an officer in place of a cash salary, from which he collected the revenue himself, was known as _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Iqta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Iqta was a revenue assignment granted to a noble or military officer in lieu of a cash salary. The holder, called an iqtadar or muqti, collected the revenue of the assigned area, kept his own pay from it, maintained a body of troops out of it, and sent the balance to the treasury. (इक्ता व्यवस्था)

 

• The system was introduced in India by Iltutmish, and was the backbone of the Sultanate's administration.

 

• Iqtas were transferable and not hereditary — the holder was moved from one assignment to another so that he could not build up a local power base. Firoz Shah Tughlaq later made them hereditary, which weakened central authority.

 

• Alauddin Khalji brought many iqtas back under direct control and paid his soldiers in cash.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other terms of Sultanate administration worth knowing:

 

• Diwan-i-Wizarat – finance; Diwan-i-Arz – military, set up by Balban

 

• Diwan-i-Risalat – religious affairs; Diwan-i-Insha – correspondence

 

• Diwan-i-Kohi – agriculture, created by Muhammad bin Tughlaq

 

• Diwan-i-Khairat – charity, and Diwan-i-Bandagan – slaves, both created by Firoz Shah Tughlaq

 

NOTE

 

• Khalisa (Option 1): Land held directly by the crown, whose revenue went straight into the royal treasury without passing through any assignee.

 

• Inam (Option 3): A revenue-free grant, usually made to scholars, holy men or those in royal favour. It carried no obligation to maintain troops.

 

• Waqf (Option 4): A religious endowment under Islamic law, in which property is dedicated in perpetuity to a charitable or pious purpose and cannot thereafter be sold or inherited.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding the Green Revolution in India is/are correct?

I. It was led in India by M.S. Swaminathan, using the high-yielding wheat varieties developed by Norman Borlaug in Mexico.
II. In its first phase it raised the output of wheat and rice alike, and did so uniformly across all the states of India.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. The Green Revolution in India was led by M.S. Swaminathan, known as the "Father of the Green Revolution in India", working with the dwarf high-yielding wheat varieties developed in Mexico by Norman Borlaug, who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. (हरित क्रांति — एम.एस. स्वामीनाथन)

 

• Statement II is INCORRECT on both counts:

 

• In its first phase (mid-1960s to mid-1970s) the gains were confined almost entirely to WHEAT. Rice responded much later, in the second phase.

 

• The gains were not uniform. They were concentrated in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh — regions that already had assured irrigation, without which the new seeds could not perform. Eastern and central India were largely left out.

 

• The programme was formally launched as the High Yielding Varieties Programme (HYVP) in 1966-67, under Agriculture Minister C. Subramaniam.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Green Revolution rested on a package — high-yielding seeds, assured irrigation, chemical fertilisers, pesticides and mechanisation. Any one element missing, and the package failed.

 

• Its criticisms: regional imbalance, benefit concentrated among larger farmers, falling water tables, soil degradation and loss of crop diversity.

 

• India's other "revolutions": White (milk, Verghese Kurien), Blue (fish), Yellow (oilseeds), Pink (prawn/onion), Golden (horticulture), Silver (eggs).

 

NOTE

 

• Since Statement I is correct and Statement II is not, Option 2 (Only II), Option 3 (Both I and II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• Statement II is a good example of a claim that is half true. Wheat output did rise sharply; but the words "and rice alike" and "uniformly across all the states" make the whole statement false. In statement questions, a single overreaching word can decide the answer.

question: The ruler Gautamiputra Satakarni belonged to which dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Satavahana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Gautamiputra Satakarni was the greatest ruler of the Satavahana dynasty, which ruled the Deccan from about the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE. (गौतमीपुत्र सातकर्णी — सातवाहन वंश)

 

• His achievements are recorded in the Nasik Prashasti, an inscription issued by his mother Gautami Balashri, which calls him the destroyer of the Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas.

 

• He defeated the Shaka ruler Nahapana and restruck Nahapana's silver coins with his own emblem — a rare and direct piece of evidence for the victory.

 

• He took the title "Ekabrahmana" and claimed to have restored the varna order.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Satavahanas are notable for the practice of metronymics — rulers named after their mothers, as *Gautami*-putra and *Vasishthi*-putra. Yet succession itself was patrilineal.

 

• Their capital was Pratishthana (Paithan) on the Godavari. Simuka founded the dynasty; Hala wrote the Gathasaptashati in Prakrit.

 

• They issued the earliest lead coins in India and built the Karle and Nasik cave complexes.

 

NOTE

 

• Kushana (Option 1): The dynasty of Kanishka, ruling the north-west from Purushapura (Peshawar). Kanishka convened the Fourth Buddhist Council and patronised the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.

 

• Vakataka (Option 2): The dynasty that succeeded the Satavahanas in the Deccan, founded by Vindhyashakti. The Ajanta paintings were largely executed under their patronage.

 

• Shunga (Option 4): Founded in 185 BCE by Pushyamitra Shunga, who killed the last Mauryan king. They enlarged the Sanchi and Bharhut stupas.

question: The ruler Mihira Bhoja, the greatest king of his line, belonged to which dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gurjara-Pratihara.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mihira Bhoja, also called Bhoja I, ruled from about 836 to 885 CE and was the greatest king of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty. (मिहिर भोज — गुर्जर-प्रतिहार वंश)

 

• His capital was Kannauj, and his empire extended from the Sutlej to Bihar and southward to the Narmada.

 

• He was a devotee of Vishnu and took the title "Adivaraha", which appears on his silver coins.

 

• The Arab traveller Sulaiman described his army, and his kingdom as one of the strongest in India at that time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Tripartite Struggle of the 8th and 9th centuries was fought for control of Kannauj between three powers:

 

• The Gurjara-Pratiharas of western India

 

• The Palas of Bengal and Bihar

 

• The Rashtrakutas of the Deccan

 

• The Pratiharas finally prevailed and held Kannauj, though the long contest exhausted all three and left northern India divided when Mahmud of Ghazni began his raids.

 

• Nagabhata I, the founder, checked the Arab advance from Sindh — for which the dynasty is remembered as a "pratihara", a doorkeeper of India.

 

NOTE

 

• Pala (Option 1): Of Bengal and Bihar, founded by Gopala and made great by Dharmapala and Devapala. They were patrons of Buddhism and founded the Vikramshila and Odantapuri monasteries.

 

• Chandela (Option 2): Of Bundelkhand, builders of the Khajuraho temples. Vidyadhara was their most powerful ruler.

 

• Rashtrakuta (Option 3): Of the Deccan, with their capital at Manyakheta. Krishna I built the Kailasa temple at Ellora, and Amoghavarsha wrote the Kavirajamarga.

question: "Thirayattam" is a ritual performing art traditionally associated with which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kerala.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Thirayattam is a ritual performing art of KERALA, practised chiefly in the Malabar region — the districts of Kozhikode and Malappuram. (तिरयाट्टम — केरल)

 

• It is performed in the courtyards of kavus (sacred groves) and village shrines, at the close of the harvest season between December and May.

 

• The performer, in elaborate costume, headgear and facial painting, is believed to become possessed by the deity he represents. The art combines dance, drama, mime, percussion and ritual.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kerala's ritual and folk performance forms are numerous and are frequently confused with one another:

 

• Theyyam – the best known, of north Malabar, in which the performer is worshipped as the deity himself

 

• Thirayattam – of the Kozhikode-Malappuram belt

 

• Mudiyettu – a ritual drama of the Bhadrakali legend, recognised by UNESCO

 

• Padayani – of central Travancore, using painted masks (*kolams*) of areca sheath

 

• Koodiyattam – Sanskrit theatre, the first Indian art form on the UNESCO list

 

NOTE

 

• Karnataka (Option 2): Known for Yakshagana, the all-night folk theatre of the coastal districts, and for Dollu Kunitha, Veeragase and Bhootha Aradhane.

 

• Tamil Nadu (Option 3): Known for the classical Bharatanatyam, and for the folk forms Therukoothu (street theatre), Karagattam, Kavadi Attam and Oyilattam.

 

• Andhra Pradesh (Option 4): Known for Kuchipudi, and for Veeranatyam, Butta Bommalu and Dhimsa.

question: "Chhapeli" is a traditional folk dance of which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uttarakhand.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Chhapeli is a traditional folk dance of UTTARAKHAND, belonging chiefly to the Kumaon region. (छपेली — उत्तराखंड)

 

• It is a romantic dance performed in pairs, a man and a woman, and is danced at weddings and at festive gatherings.

 

• The male dancer carries a mirror in one hand and a coloured handkerchief in the other, and the dance is accompanied by the hurka — a small hourglass drum from which the related form *Hurkiya Bol* takes its name.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other folk dances of Uttarakhand: Langvir Nritya (an acrobatic dance performed on a pole), Barada Nati, Jhora, Chholiya (a sword dance performed at weddings) and Chancheri.

 

• Uttarakhand became the 27th state of India on 9 November 2000. Its winter capital is Dehradun and its declared capital is Gairsain.

 

NOTE

 

• Himachal Pradesh (Option 1): Known for Nati (recognised by the Guinness records for the largest folk dance), Chham, Kayang and Dangi.

 

• Punjab (Option 3): Known for Bhangra (male) and Giddha (female), and for Jhummar, Sammi and Malwai Giddha.

 

• Haryana (Option 4): Known for Ghoomar, Khoria, Phag and Dhamal.

question: The outermost and toughest of the three membranes (meninges) that cover and protect the brain is called the _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Dura mater.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The brain and spinal cord are covered by three membranes called the meninges. From the outside inward they are: (मस्तिष्कावरण — तीन झिल्लियाँ)

 

• DURA MATER — the outermost and toughest, lying just within the skull. The name is Latin for "hard mother".

 

• ARACHNOID MATER — the middle layer, a delicate web-like membrane, so named from the Greek for "spider".

 

• PIA MATER — the innermost, a thin membrane lying directly on the surface of the brain and following all its folds. The name means "tender mother".

 

• Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulates in the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and the pia mater, and acts as a shock absorber.

 

• Inflammation of these membranes is meningitis.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The human brain weighs about 1.4 kg and has three main parts:

 

• Cerebrum – the largest part; seat of thought, memory, will and voluntary action

 

• Cerebellum – balance, posture and coordination of movement

 

• Medulla oblongata – involuntary actions: breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure, vomiting

 

• The hypothalamus regulates temperature, hunger and thirst; the pons links the parts of the brain.

 

NOTE

 

• Pia mater (Option 1): The innermost membrane, in direct contact with the brain tissue — the opposite end of the series from the one asked for.

 

• Arachnoid mater (Option 2): The middle membrane. The cerebrospinal fluid lies beneath it.

 

• Perineurium (Option 4): Not a covering of the brain at all. It is the sheath that surrounds a bundle of nerve fibres in a peripheral nerve.

question: "Mopin", the festival of prosperity marked by the smearing of rice flour and the Popir dance, is celebrated by the Galo community of which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arunachal Pradesh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mopin is the principal festival of the Galo community of ARUNACHAL PRADESH, celebrated chiefly in the West Siang district. (मोपिन — अरुणाचल प्रदेश)

 

• It is held in April, and is a festival of prosperity and of protection from evil and disease, invoking the goddess Mopin Ane.

 

• Its two distinguishing features are the smearing of rice flour (etor) on the faces of participants as a mark of purity and good fortune, and the Popir dance, performed by women in white.

 

• Apong, the local rice beer, is prepared and distributed through the community during the festival.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Arunachal Pradesh is home to 26 major tribes, and nearly every one has its own festival:

 

• Solung – the Adis, in September

 

• Nyokum – the Nyishis, in February

 

• Dree – the Apatanis, an agricultural festival in July

 

• Losar – the Monpas, the Buddhist new year

 

• Boori Boot – the Hill Miris

 

• Arunachal Pradesh became a full state on 20 February 1987, on the same day as Mizoram. Its capital is Itanagar.

 

NOTE

 

• Nagaland (Option 1): Known for the Hornbill Festival, held each December at Kisama and called the "festival of festivals", and for Moatsu of the Aos and Aoling of the Konyaks.

 

• Mizoram (Option 2): Known for its three *Kuts* — Chapchar Kut in March, Mim Kut and Pawl Kut.

 

• Sikkim (Option 3): Known for Losoong, Saga Dawa and Pang Lhabsol, honouring Mount Khangchendzonga as the guardian deity.

question: The "Bhagoria" festival, held just before Holi and known for its village fairs, is celebrated chiefly by which tribal community of Madhya Pradesh?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bhils.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Bhagoria festival is celebrated by the BHIL and Bhilala communities of the Jhabua, Alirajpur, Dhar and Khargone districts of western Madhya Pradesh. (भगोरिया — भील जनजाति)

 

• It is held in the week immediately before Holi, in March, when the harvest is in and the fields are free.

 

• It takes the form of a series of haats or village fairs, at which young men and women meet, dance to the dhol and mandal, and — by long custom — choose their own partners. The festival is thus both a harvest fair and a courtship gathering.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Bhils are among the largest tribal communities in India, spread over Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. Their traditional wall painting is the Pithora.

 

• Major tribes and their states: Gond (Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh), Santhal (Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha), Bhil (western India), Toda (Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu), Munda and Oraon (Jharkhand), Khasi, Garo and Jaintia (Meghalaya), Bodo (Assam), Jarawa and Sentinelese (Andaman).

 

NOTE

 

• Gonds (Option 1): Also of Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh, and numerically the largest tribe of central India. Their festivals are Keslapur Jatra and Madai, and their painting tradition is Gond art.

 

• Todas (Option 2): A small pastoral community of the Nilgiri hills in Tamil Nadu, known for their barrel-vaulted huts and their reverence for the buffalo — not a Madhya Pradesh tribe at all.

 

• Santhals (Option 3): Of Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha. Their festivals are Sohrai and Baha, and they led the Santhal Rebellion of 1855 under Sidhu and Kanhu.

question: What is the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha as laid down by the Constitution of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 250.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Article 80 of the Constitution fixes the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha at 250. (राज्य सभा की अधिकतम सदस्य संख्या — 250)

 

• This maximum is made up of:

 

• Not more than 238 representatives of the States and Union Territories, elected indirectly

 

• 12 members nominated by the President for special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service

 

• The actual present strength is 245 — 233 elected and 12 nominated. The gap between 245 and 250 exists because the constitutional ceiling allows room for future states.

 

• Members of the Rajya Sabha are elected by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, by proportional representation with a single transferable vote.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Rajya Sabha is a permanent body and cannot be dissolved. One-third of its members retire every two years, each member serving a term of six years.

 

• The Vice-President of India is its ex-officio Chairman, though he is not a member of the House.

 

• Compare the Lok Sabha: maximum strength 550 under Article 81 — 530 from the States and 20 from the Union Territories. The provision for two nominated Anglo-Indian members was discontinued by the 104th Amendment (2019).

 

NOTE

 

• 233 (Option 1): The number of elected members at present — the representatives of the States and Union Territories. It excludes the 12 nominated members.

 

• 245 (Option 2): The present actual strength, 233 + 12. This is the most tempting answer, and the question turns precisely on the difference between the present strength and the constitutional ceiling.

 

• 252 (Option 4): Not a figure that appears anywhere in the constitutional scheme for the Rajya Sabha.

question: Which of the following statements is NOT correct regarding the force of gravitation?
option_1: The gravitational force between two bodies is directly proportional to the product of their masses.
option_2: The gravitational force between two bodies is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
option_3: The value of the universal gravitational constant G is the same everywhere in the universe.
option_4: The value of the acceleration due to gravity g is the same at every point on the surface of the earth.
solution_text:
The correct answer is The value of the acceleration due to gravity g is the same at every point on the surface of the earth.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This statement is NOT correct. The value of g VARIES from place to place on the earth's surface. (g का मान सर्वत्र समान नहीं होता)

 

• g is maximum at the POLES (about 9.83 m/s²) and minimum at the EQUATOR (about 9.78 m/s²), for two reasons acting together:

 

• The earth is not a perfect sphere — it is flattened at the poles and bulges at the equator, so the polar radius is smaller and g correspondingly greater.

 

• The rotation of the earth produces an effect that reduces the apparent weight of a body, and this effect is greatest at the equator and zero at the poles.

 

• g also decreases with altitude as one goes above the surface, and decreases with depth as one goes below it, becoming zero at the centre of the earth.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Newton's law of universal gravitation: F = G m₁m₂ / r²

 

• G is the universal gravitational constant, whose value is 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Its value is fixed everywhere, which is why it is called *universal*.

 

• The average value of g taken for calculation is 9.8 m/s².

 

• On the Moon, g is about one-sixth of its value on the earth. Mass is constant everywhere; weight (W = mg) changes with g.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 is correct. F ∝ m₁m₂ — doubling either mass doubles the force.

 

• Option 2 is correct. F ∝ 1/r² — this is the inverse-square law, so doubling the distance reduces the force to a quarter.

 

• Option 3 is correct. G is a universal constant; it does not depend on the masses, the distance, or the medium between the bodies. Note the distinction from g, which is not a constant at all — confusing the two is exactly what this question tests.

question: Who led the Revolt of 1857 at Faizabad and was among its most prominent religious leaders?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah, of Faizabad, was among the ablest and most feared leaders of the Revolt of 1857. (मौलवी अहमदुल्लाह शाह — फैजाबाद)

 

• He was called the "Lighthouse of Rebellion" in Awadh, and had preached against British rule from mosque to mosque well before the outbreak, being imprisoned for it.

 

• He led the rebel forces at the Battle of Chinhat (June 1857), in which the British were defeated, and afterwards played a leading part in the siege of the Lucknow Residency.

 

• He was killed in June 1858 by the Raja of Powayan, who was paid a reward of Rs 50,000 for his head.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Leaders of the Revolt of 1857 and their centres:

 

• Delhi – Bahadur Shah Zafar, with General Bakht Khan

 

• Lucknow – Begum Hazrat Mahal

 

• Kanpur – Nana Saheb, with Tantia Tope

 

• Jhansi – Rani Lakshmibai

 

• Bareilly – Khan Bahadur Khan

 

• Bihar (Jagdishpur) – Kunwar Singh

 

• Faizabad – Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah

 

• Allahabad – Liaquat Ali

 

• The Governor-General at the time was Lord Canning, who became the first Viceroy after the Government of India Act, 1858 transferred power from the Company to the Crown.

 

NOTE

 

• Kunwar Singh (Option 1): The aged zamindar of Jagdishpur in Bihar, who took up the revolt at nearly eighty and conducted a remarkable campaign before dying of his wounds in April 1858.

 

• Khan Bahadur Khan (Option 3): Leader of the revolt at Bareilly in Rohilkhand, a descendant of the Rohilla chiefs.

 

• Rao Tula Ram (Option 4): Leader of the revolt in Rewari, in present-day Haryana, who fought the British at Nasibpur and later sought help abroad.

question: The Kirana Gharana of Hindustani classical music was founded by _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ustad Abdul Karim Khan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kirana Gharana was founded by Ustad Abdul Karim Khan (1872-1937), together with his cousin Ustad Abdul Wahid Khan. (किराना घराना — उस्ताद अब्दुल करीम खाँ)

 

• The gharana takes its name from Kairana, a town in the Shamli district of western Uttar Pradesh.

 

• Its distinguishing feature is the slow, meditative elaboration of each note (swara), with great emphasis on precise intonation and on the unhurried unfolding of the raga.

 

• Its most celebrated later exponents were Pandit Bhimsen Joshi, Gangubai Hangal, Sawai Gandharva and Prabha Atre.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The principal gharanas of Hindustani vocal music:

 

• Gwalior – the oldest gharana of khayal, founded by Nathan Peer Bakhsh

 

• Kirana – Abdul Karim Khan; known for slow, note-centred elaboration

 

• Jaipur-Atrauli – Ustad Alladiya Khan; known for complex, rare ragas

 

• Agra – known for its forceful, rhythmic style; Ustad Faiyaz Khan

 

• Patiala – Ali Bakhsh and Fateh Ali; Bade Ghulam Ali Khan

 

• Rampur-Sahaswan and Bhendibazaar

 

• The word gharana comes from *ghar*, "house", and denotes a lineage of musical training passed from guru to disciple.

 

NOTE

 

• Ustad Alladiya Khan (Option 2): Founder of the Jaipur-Atrauli Gharana, known for intricate, elaborately constructed ragas. He is the closest distractor here.

 

• Ustad Faiyaz Khan (Option 3): The greatest exponent of the Agra Gharana, celebrated for a robust, dhrupad-influenced style.

 

• Pandit Vishnu Digambar Paluskar (Option 4): Not the founder of a gharana but a great reformer, who founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya in 1901 and brought classical music out of the courts into public teaching.

question: In which year did the Cripps Mission arrive in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1942.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Cripps Mission, headed by Sir Stafford Cripps, arrived in India in March 1942. (क्रिप्स मिशन — 1942)

 

• It was sent by the British War Cabinet under Winston Churchill at a moment of crisis: Japan had entered the war, Singapore and Rangoon had fallen, and Indian cooperation was urgently needed.

 

• Its offer was of Dominion Status after the war, with an elected body to frame a new constitution, and the right of any province to stay out of the proposed Union.

 

• The Congress rejected it because the offer was deferred to the end of the war and gave no immediate share in power. Gandhi called it "a post-dated cheque" — to which the phrase *on a crashing bank* is popularly added.

 

• The failure of the mission led directly to the Quit India Movement of August 1942.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• British missions and their years:

 

• Simon Commission – 1928; all-white, hence "Simon Go Back"

 

• Round Table Conferences – 1930, 1931, 1932

 

• August Offer – 1940

 

• Cripps Mission – 1942

 

• Wavell Plan / Simla Conference – 1945

 

• Cabinet Mission – 1946

 

• Mountbatten Plan – 3 June 1947

 

NOTE

 

• 1935 (Option 1): The year of the Government of India Act, 1935, which introduced provincial autonomy and is a principal source of the present Constitution.

 

• 1940 (Option 2): The year of the August Offer, and of the Lahore Resolution of the Muslim League.

 

• 1946 (Option 4): The year of the Cabinet Mission, which proposed a three-tier federal structure and led to the formation of the Constituent Assembly and the Interim Government.

question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding the river Godavari?
option_1: It is the longest river of peninsular India.
option_2: It rises near Trimbakeshwar in the Nashik district of Maharashtra.
option_3: Its principal tributaries include the Pravara, Manjra, Penganga, Wardha, Wainganga and Indravati.
option_4: It is known as the Dakshina Ganga because it flows westward and drains into the Arabian Sea.
solution_text:
The correct answer is It is known as the Dakshina Ganga because it flows westward and drains into the Arabian Sea.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• This statement is INCORRECT, and it is worth seeing exactly why. The Godavari is indeed called the "Dakshina Ganga" — but the reason given is false. (गोदावरी — दक्षिण गंगा)

 

• The Godavari flows EASTWARD and drains into the BAY OF BENGAL, forming a large delta in Andhra Pradesh. It does not flow west, and does not reach the Arabian Sea.

 

• It is called the *Dakshina Ganga* because of its length, its sanctity and the size of its basin — it is the Ganga of the south — not because of the direction of its flow.

 

• The Narmada and the Tapi are the two major peninsular rivers that do flow westward into the Arabian Sea, through rift valleys.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Godavari is 1,465 km long, the longest river of peninsular India and the second longest in India after the Ganga.

 

• Its basin covers about 10% of India's area, spread over Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Karnataka and Puducherry (Yanam).

 

• Projects on it: the Polavaram project and the Sriram Sagar project. The Kumbh Mela is held at Nashik on its banks.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 is correct. At 1,465 km the Godavari is the longest of the peninsular rivers, ahead of the Krishna (1,400 km) and the Mahanadi.

 

• Option 2 is correct. It rises at Trimbakeshwar, near Nashik in Maharashtra, in the Western Ghats, at a height of about 1,067 m.

 

• Option 3 is correct. Those are its principal tributaries; the Indravati, Wainganga and Manjra are among the largest of them.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding national income aggregates is/are correct?

I. Net National Product at factor cost is also known as National Income.
II. Gross National Product is obtained by adding net factor income from abroad to Gross Domestic Product.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. Net National Product at factor cost (NNP at FC) is precisely what is meant by National Income. (राष्ट्रीय आय — साधन लागत पर शुद्ध राष्ट्रीय उत्पाद)

 

• It is called net because depreciation (the consumption of fixed capital) has been deducted, and at factor cost because indirect taxes have been deducted and subsidies added back, so that what remains is the income actually received by the factors of production — rent, wages, interest and profit.

 

• Statement II is CORRECT. GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA).

 

• GDP measures what is produced within the geographical boundary of the country, whoever produces it.

 

• GNP measures what is produced by the residents of the country, wherever they are.

 

• NFIA is the income earned by Indian residents abroad minus the income earned by foreigners in India. For India, NFIA is usually negative, so India's GNP is generally less than its GDP.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The chain of aggregates:

 

• GDP at MP − depreciation = NDP at MP

 

• GDP at MP + NFIA = GNP at MP

 

• GNP at MP − depreciation = NNP at MP

 

• NNP at MP − indirect taxes + subsidies = NNP at FC = NATIONAL INCOME

 

• Per capita income = National Income ÷ Population.

 

• In India these estimates are prepared by the National Statistical Office (NSO), under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation. The base year currently in use is 2011-12.

 

NOTE

 

• Since both statements are correct, Option 1 (Only I), Option 2 (Only II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• The two ideas being tested are distinct and should not be run together: "net" versus "gross" turns on depreciation, while "national" versus "domestic" turns on NFIA. Keeping those two axes separate makes the whole family of aggregates straightforward.

question: Who are the authors of the book "Poor Economics: A Radical Rethinking of the Way to Fight Global Poverty"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Poor Economics" was published in 2011 and written jointly by Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo. (पुअर इकोनॉमिक्स — अभिजीत बनर्जी एवं एस्थर डुफ्लो)

 

• Its argument is that poverty should be studied not through grand theory but through randomised controlled trials (RCTs) — small, carefully designed field experiments that test what actually changes behaviour among the poor.

 

• The two authors, together with Michael Kremer, were awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2019 for exactly this experimental approach to alleviating global poverty.

 

• Abhijit Banerjee is the second Indian-origin economist to receive the prize, after Amartya Sen (1998).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Banerjee and Duflo also wrote "Good Economics for Hard Times" (2019). They co-founded the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) at MIT.

 

• Books by Indian economists worth knowing: "Development as Freedom" and "The Argumentative Indian" (Amartya Sen), "An Uncertain Glory" (Drèze and Sen), "I Do What I Do" and "Fault Lines" (Raghuram Rajan), "An Economist at Home and Abroad" (Shankar Acharya).

 

NOTE

 

• Raghuram Rajan and Rohit Lamba (Option 1): Joint authors of "Breaking the Mould: Reimagining India's Economic Future" (2024). Rajan is a former Governor of the RBI and Chief Economist of the IMF.

 

• Jean Drèze and Amartya Sen (Option 2): Joint authors of "An Uncertain Glory: India and its Contradictions" and of "India: Development and Participation".

 

• Kaushik Basu and Arvind Subramanian (Option 4): Both former Chief Economic Advisers to the Government of India. Basu wrote "An Economist in the Real World"; Subramanian wrote "Of Counsel".

question: Who is the author of the book "The Other Side of Silence: Voices from the Partition of India"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Urvashi Butalia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The Other Side of Silence: Voices from the Partition of India" (1998) was written by Urvashi Butalia. (द अदर साइड ऑफ साइलेंस — उर्वशी बुटालिया)

 

• It is an oral history of Partition, built from interviews with survivors, and it recovers the experience of those whom the political narrative had left out — women, children, Dalits and the abducted.

 

• Its central claim is that the official history of Partition records the transfer of power but is silent on the human cost, which survives only in memory and in family silence.

 

• The book won the Oral History Book Association Award and is a standard work on the subject.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Urvashi Butalia co-founded Kali for Women, India's first feminist publishing house, in 1984, and later founded Zubaan. She received the Padma Shri in 2011.

 

• Other important works on Partition: "Borders and Boundaries" (Ritu Menon and Kamla Bhasin), "Remnants of a Separation" (Aanchal Malhotra), "Train to Pakistan" (Khushwant Singh), "Tamas" (Bhisham Sahni) and the short story "Toba Tek Singh" (Saadat Hasan Manto).

 

NOTE

 

• Anita Desai (Option 1): A novelist, three times shortlisted for the Booker Prize, author of "Clear Light of Day", "In Custody" and "Fire on the Mountain". She writes fiction, not oral history.

 

• Ritu Menon (Option 2): Co-author of "Borders and Boundaries" and co-founder, with Urvashi Butalia, of Kali for Women. She is the closest distractor, since the two worked on the same subject in the same years.

 

• Kamla Bhasin (Option 3): A feminist activist and poet, best known for the slogan and song "Azadi", and co-author with Ritu Menon of "Borders and Boundaries: Women in India's Partition".

question: Rani ki Vav, the eleventh-century stepwell inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014, is located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gujarat.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rani ki Vav ("the Queen's Stepwell") is at Patan, in GUJARAT, on the bank of the Saraswati river. (रानी की वाव — पाटन, गुजरात)

 

• It was built in the 11th century by Queen Udayamati in memory of her husband Bhima I of the Solanki (Chaulukya) dynasty.

 

• It is built in the Maru-Gurjara style, on seven levels of stairs, and carries over 500 principal sculptures — the largest group being the ten incarnations (Dashavatara) of Vishnu.

 

• Silted over by the Saraswati for centuries, it was excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India in the 1980s, which is why its carving survives in such condition.

 

• It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014, and appears on the Rs 100 currency note.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Gujarat: Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park, Rani ki Vav (Patan), the Historic City of Ahmedabad (India's first World Heritage City, 2017), and Dholavira (2021).

 

• Other famous stepwells: Adalaj ni Vav near Ahmedabad, Chand Baori at Abhaneri in Rajasthan, and Agrasen ki Baoli in Delhi.

 

NOTE

 

• Rajasthan (Option 1): The likeliest wrong answer, since Rajasthan has many celebrated stepwells, including Chand Baori and Panna Meena ka Kund — but Rani ki Vav is not among them.

 

• Madhya Pradesh (Option 3): Its World Heritage Sites are Khajuraho, Sanchi and the Bhimbetka rock shelters.

 

• Maharashtra (Option 4): Its World Heritage Sites include Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta and the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus.

question: Which of the following is India's only "mixed" UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed for both its natural and its cultural value?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Khangchendzonga National Park.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Khangchendzonga National Park in Sikkim is India's only MIXED World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2016. (कंचनजंगा राष्ट्रीय उद्यान — मिश्रित विश्व धरोहर स्थल)

 

• UNESCO recognises three classes of site — cultural, natural and mixed. A mixed site must satisfy at least one criterion from each of the other two lists, which is why such sites are rare: there are only about 40 in the world.

 

• Khangchendzonga qualifies on natural grounds for its glaciers, forests and biodiversity, and on cultural grounds because the mountain is revered by the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples as a guardian deity, and the park contains sacred caves, lakes and pilgrimage routes.

 

• Kangchenjunga itself, at 8,586 m, is the third highest mountain in the world and the highest in India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's natural World Heritage Sites: Kaziranga, Manas, Keoladeo, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers, Western Ghats, and the Great Himalayan National Park.

 

• The first Indian sites, all inscribed in 1983, were Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal.

 

• The Maratha Military Landscapes were India's most recent inscription, in 2025.

 

NOTE

 

• Sundarbans National Park (Option 1): Inscribed in 1987 as a natural site — the largest mangrove forest in the world and the home of the Royal Bengal tiger. It is not a mixed site.

 

• Kaziranga National Park (Option 3): Inscribed in 1985 as a natural site, in Assam, holding about two-thirds of the world's one-horned rhinoceroses.

 

• Western Ghats (Option 4): Inscribed in 2012 as a natural site, a serial listing of 39 properties across six states, and one of the world's eight "hottest hotspots" of biological diversity.

question: Which of the following statements correctly describes a "keystone species"?
option_1: A species whose removal would produce a disproportionately large change in the structure of its ecosystem
option_2: A species that is the most numerous of all the species in its ecosystem
option_3: A species that has been introduced into an ecosystem from another country
option_4: A species that occupies the top position in every food chain of its ecosystem
solution_text:
The correct answer is A species whose removal would produce a disproportionately large change in the structure of its ecosystem.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A keystone species is one whose effect on its ecosystem is out of all proportion to its abundance. Remove it, and the structure of the whole community alters. (आधारशिला प्रजाति)

 

• The name is taken from architecture: the keystone is the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch which, though it bears little weight itself, holds all the other stones in place. Take it out and the arch falls.

 

• The decisive point is influence, not numbers. A keystone species is frequently not the commonest species in its habitat, and may be quite rare.

 

• Standard examples: the sea otter, which keeps down sea urchins and so preserves the kelp forest; the tiger as apex predator; the elephant, which keeps grassland open by pushing over trees; and the fig tree, which fruits when little else does and so sustains many animals through the lean season.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Related terms in ecology, often confused with this one:

 

• Endemic species – found naturally in one geographical area and nowhere else

 

• Indicator species – whose presence or condition signals the health of the ecosystem, such as lichens for air quality

 

• Flagship species – chosen to attract public support for conservation, such as the tiger or the panda

 

• Umbrella species – whose protection incidentally protects many others sharing its habitat

 

• Invasive alien species – introduced from elsewhere and spreading to the harm of native species

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 confuses influence with abundance. The commonest species is the dominant species, which is not the same thing — a keystone species is often scarce.

 

• Option 3 describes an introduced or alien species, which may indeed alter an ecosystem, but does so as an invader rather than as a support of the existing structure.

 

• Option 4 describes an apex predator. Many keystone species are apex predators, but not all — the fig tree and the elephant are keystone species and neither is a predator at all. The definition turns on effect, not on position in the food chain.

question: "Alha", the heroic ballad sung of the deeds of the warriors Alha and Udal, belongs to which region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bundelkhand.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alha (or Alha-Khand) is the great heroic ballad of BUNDELKHAND, the region spread across southern Uttar Pradesh and northern Madhya Pradesh. (आल्हा — बुंदेलखंड)

 

• It celebrates the deeds of the brothers Alha and Udal, warriors in the service of Raja Parmal (Paramardideva) of the Chandela kingdom of Mahoba, who fought against Prithviraj Chauhan in the twelfth century.

 

• It is traditionally sung in the rainy season, in a loud, vigorous style, to the accompaniment of the dholak, and a full recitation may run for many nights.

 

• The singer is called an Alhaiti, and the metre in which it is composed is itself known as the Alha chhand.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Regional song and ballad traditions of northern and central India:

 

• Alha – Bundelkhand, heroic ballad

 

• Pandavani – Chhattisgarh, the Mahabharata narrated in song; Teejan Bai its best-known exponent

 

• Panihari – Rajasthan, sung by women fetching water

 

• Birha – Bhojpur region, songs of separation

 

• Nirgun and Kajri – eastern Uttar Pradesh

 

NOTE

 

• Kumaon (Option 1): The Uttarakhand region whose traditions are Jhora, Chhapeli, Bair and the auspicious Shakunakhar songs sung at weddings and births.

 

• Vidarbha (Option 3): The eastern region of Maharashtra, whose folk forms are Gondhal, Bharud and Dandar.

 

• Malwa (Option 4): The plateau region of western Madhya Pradesh, known for Nirgun bhajans, Kanagat songs and the Malwi Lok Geet tradition.

question: The infoldings of the inner membrane of the mitochondrion, which greatly increase its surface area, are called _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Cristae.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The mitochondrion has two membranes. The outer membrane is smooth; the inner membrane is thrown into deep folds called CRISTAE (singular *crista*). (क्रिस्टी — माइटोकॉन्ड्रिया की आंतरिक झिल्ली की वलनें)

 

• The purpose of the folding is to increase the surface area available for the enzymes and carriers of the electron transport chain, which are embedded in that membrane. The greater the area, the more ATP can be produced.

 

• The space enclosed by the inner membrane is the matrix, where the Krebs cycle takes place.

 

• The mitochondrion is called the "powerhouse of the cell" because it is the site of aerobic respiration and of most ATP synthesis.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mitochondria are semi-autonomous organelles: they possess their own circular DNA and ribosomes, and can make some of their own proteins. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the mother alone.

 

• Cells with high energy demands — heart muscle, liver, nerve cells — contain the largest numbers of mitochondria. Mature mammalian red blood cells have none at all.

 

NOTE

 

• Thylakoids (Option 1): Flattened membranous sacs inside the chloroplast, not the mitochondrion. They contain chlorophyll and are the site of the light reaction of photosynthesis.

 

• Villi (Option 2): Not a cell organelle at all. Villi are the finger-like projections of the inner wall of the small intestine, which increase the surface area for the absorption of digested food.

 

• Grana (Option 3): Stacks of thylakoids within the chloroplast. This and the previous option belong to the plant cell's photosynthetic machinery, and are placed here because they perform the analogous job of increasing membrane surface area — but in a different organelle.

question: Which is the largest nuclear power station in India by installed capacity?
option_2: Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant, Tamil Nadu
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant, Tamil Nadu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant, in the Tirunelveli district of Tamil Nadu, is the largest nuclear power station in India by installed capacity. (कुडनकुलम — भारत का सबसे बड़ा परमाणु ऊर्जा संयंत्र)

 

• Its two operating units are of 1,000 MW each, giving 2,000 MW in all — more than any other Indian station.

 

• It is built with Russian cooperation and uses VVER pressurised water reactors, which differ from the pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWRs) used at most other Indian stations.

 

• Unit 1 attained criticality in 2013 and Unit 2 in 2016; further units are under construction, which will take the site to 6,000 MW.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nuclear power stations in India and their states:

 

• Tarapur – Maharashtra (the first, commissioned in 1969)

 

• Rawatbhata – Rajasthan; Kakrapar – Gujarat

 

• Kalpakkam (Madras) – Tamil Nadu; Kudankulam – Tamil Nadu

 

• Narora – Uttar Pradesh; Kaiga – Karnataka

 

• All are operated by the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL).

 

• India's three-stage nuclear programme was framed by Homi J. Bhabha: stage one uses natural uranium in PHWRs, stage two plutonium in fast breeder reactors, and stage three thorium, of which India holds among the largest reserves in the world.

 

NOTE

 

• Tarapur (Option 1): India's first nuclear power station, commissioned in 1969 with American help. It is the oldest but not the largest, with a total capacity of about 1,400 MW.

 

• Kakrapar (Option 3): In Gujarat, notable for Unit 3, India's first indigenously designed 700 MW PHWR, which began commercial operation in 2023.

 

• Rajasthan Atomic Power Station, Rawatbhata (Option 4): Has the largest number of units of any Indian station, but its total capacity is lower than Kudankulam's.
